sections.heading: 4.7 Robustness Checks
sections.text: The core findings could depend on the single-surrogate linear DGPs; the checks below vary the number of surrogates, the functional form, the sign of the surrogate effect, and the learner. With three surrogates (DGP 7) the surrogate index attains RE 5.36 × 5.36\times at π L = 0.05 \pi_{L}=0.05 with coverage 0.952 0.952 , inside the R = 500 R=500 band [ 0.931 , 0.969 ] [0.931,0.969] , and PPI++ keeps its guarantee at RE 1.2 1.2 – 1.4 × 1.4\times (Table A9 ). Under best-case historical calibration the composite proxy reaches 6.30 × 6.30\times in the same cell, against the surrogate index’s 5.36 × 5.36\times (ESS multipliers 39.7 39.7 and 28.7 28.7 ). An independent R = 500 R=500 run with a separately drawn library of 30 30 rather than 50 50 past experiments puts the composite proxy at 7.01 × 7.01\times and the surrogate index at 5.46 × 5.46\times (Table A26 ). Each run conditions on one realized library and does not average over the estimation uncertainty of that library, so the composite-proxy figures are best cases that depend on the library, not point estimates. Under the concave link of DGP 8 the surrogate index attains RE 5.5 × 5.5\times at π L = 0.05 \pi_{L}=0.05 with bias 0.002 0.002 and coverage 0.934 0.934 , inside the R = 500 R=500 band, and PPI++ and AIPW keep valid coverage (Table A26 ). Dropping S 2 S^{2} from the prediction model under DGP 8, where surrogacy holds by construction, leaves the two-sided diagnostic rejecting at α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 on 5.2%, 5.4%, and 5.7% of replications at π L = 0.05 \pi_{L}=0.05 , 0.20 0.20 , and 0.50 0.50 ( R = 1,000 R=1{,}000 , Monte Carlo standard error about 0.007; replication package): the diagnostic cannot see this misspecification. Its null remains joint, surrogacy together with correct specification, so a rejection is not attributable to surrogacy failure alone, and a non-rejection certifies neither component. Under the antagonistic surrogate of DGP 9 the surrogate index estimates − 0.09 -0.09 against the true 0.41 0.41 , the wrong sign, with 0% coverage; the diagnostic rejects in every replication and the hybrid reverts to PPI++ (Table A27 ). Clipping the coefficient to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] binds here, but at the simulated effect sizes it moves RMSE by 0.03 % 0.03\% at π L = 0.05 \pi_{L}=0.05 and leaves RE at 1.20 1.20 (Table A16 ). In DGP 10 the relative surrogate-index bias tracks approximately − ρ -\rho , at − 0.8 % -0.8\% , − 19.4 % -19.4\% , and − 39.7 % -39.7\% for ρ = 0 \rho=0 , 0.2 0.2 , and 0.4 0.4 at π L = 0.20 \pi_{L}=0.20 (Table A24 ), so nonlinearity and partial mediation act approximately additively; the relation is approximate even under linearity, where the bias is − δ ​ κ -\delta\kappa (Proposition 1 ). PPI++ remains unbiased throughout; the hybrid was not run on this DGP.

sections.heading: Bias versus omitted interval uncertainty.
sections.text: A surrogate index can miss the truth because a surrogacy violation biases its estimand, because the prediction model is misspecified, or because its interval omits the first-stage uncertainty of Equation ( 11 ). Recomputing every SI interval with the narrower variances, on the same point estimates, isolates the third (Table A17 ). In the linear Gaussian designs the omitted term is 0.4 to 7.2% of the joint sandwich variance and moves coverage by at most 0.008; it does not rescue SI under violation (0.678 against 0.682 at ρ = 0.2 \rho=0.2 , 0.019 against 0.021 at ρ = 0.4 \rho=0.4 ), so the collapse of Section 4.2 is bias, not a missing variance term. The Criteo-calibrated rich index of Table 14 , which adds a treatment-responsive engagement proxy to the visit indicator, is the exception: the first-stage term is 71% of the sandwich variance at m = 1 m=1 , where the rich index’s relative bias is − 0.4 % -0.4\% , and the plug-in interval covers 0.665 0.665 against the sandwich’s 0.960 0.960 , an interval defect; at m = 0.5 m=0.5 and m = 0 m=0 the sandwich still covers only 0.800 0.800 and 0.414 0.414 , which is bias. That index is exactly rank-deficient ( S 1 2 = S 1 S_{1}^{2}=S_{1} ), and relative eigenvalue floors from 10 − 8 10^{-8} to 10 − 16 10^{-16} give the same first-stage share ( 70.9 % 70.9\% ), variance ratio, coverage, and size to every reported digit, because d 0 d_{0} and every design row are orthogonal to the discarded direction (replication package). Whenever the index leans on a predictor that treatment moves, the first-stage term should be carried; it does not restore coverage where the estimand itself is wrong. Re-running representative DGPs with gradient-boosted trees leaves the method ordering unchanged (Table A10 ): the surrogate index keeps its efficiency under valid surrogacy (RE 5.59 5.59 with either model at DGP 1, π L = 0.05 \pi_{L}=0.05 ) and its collapse under violation (coverage 0.030 0.030 with OLS and 0.010 0.010 with GBT at DGP 2, ρ = 0.4 \rho=0.4 , π L = 0.20 \pi_{L}=0.20 ), while PPI++ stays within the band except under OLS at DGP 8 with π L = 0.50 \pi_{L}=0.50 ( 0.915 0.915 ; GBT 0.920 0.920 , at the band edge). GBT loses a little efficiency rather than gaining any: across the surrogate-index, PPI++, and AIPW cells of the full comparison (replication package) its RE never exceeds the OLS RE by more than 0.02 0.02 and falls as much as 14% below it, so the efficiency gap between the two families is structural, not model-driven. Trees have no coefficient expansion, so the GBT surrogate-index interval uses the fixed-predictor plug-in variance and is heuristic; on two cells it is 0.95 0.95 and 1.13 1.13 of the Monte Carlo variance, and a tree-refitting bootstrap that keeps every copy of a resampled unit in its unit’s fold agrees on the DGP 1 cell (Appendix F.3 ). The comparison’s evidential weight is therefore on bias, RMSE, and RE.

sections.heading: 4.8 The Adaptive Hybrid Estimator
sections.text: A hard-switch rule would choose between SI and PPI++; the exploratory hybrid instead combines them continuously. It reports w ​ τ ^ SI + ( 1 − w ) ​ τ ^ PPI + + w\,\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{SI}}+(1-w)\,\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{PPI++}} with the Cauchy-kernel weight w = c / ( c + T n 2 ) w=c/(c+T_{n}^{2}) at c = 1.5 c=1.5 , so the weight slides from the surrogate index toward PPI++ as the estimator-disagreement statistic grows, and it pairs that point estimate with an interval calibrated by simulation from the sandwich Σ ^ \hat{\Sigma} of Proposition 3 (Appendix A ). In the canonical R = 2,000 R=2{,}000 hybrid evaluation, under valid surrogacy (DGP 1) the hybrid attains RE 2.0 2.0 – 2.2 × 2.2\times at π L = 0.05 \pi_{L}=0.05 – 0.20 0.20 with 94–96% coverage, against the surrogate index’s 2.9 2.9 – 5.5 × 5.5\times in the same cells (Table 4 ), the gap being the efficiency cost of hedging. At the featured violation cell (DGP 2, ρ = 0.2 \rho=0.2 , π L = 0.20 \pi_{L}=0.20 ) it carries − 8.4 % -8.4\% relative bias at 0.934 0.934 coverage, and under DGP 9 its weight is near zero (mean 0.012 0.012 at π L = 0.20 \pi_{L}=0.20 ), so it reverts to PPI++. On Hillstrom the diagnostic rejects on 11.4% of splits, the mean weight stays at 0.64 0.64 , and the hybrid inherits 10.7% relative bias at 93.0% coverage (Table A22 ). Appendix A gives its limit-experiment risk (Proposition 7 ), the diverging- c n c_{n} variant, and the status of the interval, which inherits PPI++ validity under fixed detectable alternatives while we make no consistency claim at fixed c c (Remark 4 ).

sections.heading: 5 Public-Data Illustrations
sections.text: Three public experiments, spanning 445 to 13,979,592 units, illustrate the simulation findings without proprietary data. On the Hillstrom email-marketing experiment ( n = 64,000 n=64{,}000 ) the surrogate index fails while PPI++ remains valid, and, as in the detection-damage gap of Section 4.3 , the violation damages the surrogate index while the diagnostic rarely flags it. The Criteo uplift experiment ( n = 13.98 n=13.98 million) shows the same funnel violation at industrial scale, where the diagnostic detects it. Effect sizes, outcome rarity, and variances in both datasets differ from DGP 2’s. A testbed calibrated to the Criteo funnel places the observed violation on a dial, and the LaLonde experiment ( n = 445 n=445 ) is a negative control in which the “surrogate” is a pre-treatment covariate. The experiments are fixed datasets, so we mask outcomes at random to create labeled-unlabeled splits and measure how well each estimator recovers the full-sample difference in means, which we call the masking target. Coverage against it is a recovery diagnostic, not repeated-sampling coverage of the causal ATE: the target is itself an estimate that the labeled subsample overlaps, which makes labeled-only and PPI++ coverage conservative. Every bias and coverage figure in Sections 5.1 , 5.2 , and 5.4 is measured against the masking target; the semi-synthetic testbed of Section 5.3 , whose true τ \tau is known, supplies known-truth validation. Random masking makes MCAR hold by construction, so these analyses illustrate estimator behavior on real outcome distributions rather than validating the labeling mechanism.

sections.heading: 5.1 Hillstrom email marketing experiment
sections.text: This instantiates the e-commerce example as a conversion funnel. The Hillstrom data ( Hillstrom, 2008 ) , accessed via scikit-uplift, cover 64,000 customers randomized in equal thirds to a men’s merchandise campaign, a women’s merchandise campaign, or no email. We pool the two campaigns (treatment n 1 = 42,694 n_{1}=42{,}694 ; control n 0 = 21,306 n_{0}=21{,}306 ), so the estimand is the effect of receiving either campaign. The surrogate is a binary website visit within two weeks and the outcome is conversion (a purchase); both are recorded over the same two-week window, so the data exercise the funnel structure rather than calendar maturation. Visits are roughly sixteen to nineteen times as common as conversions, and every conversion follows a visit, a fact about how events are recorded rather than identification of a mediation mechanism. Treatment also raises the conversion rate among visitors, from 5.4% to 6.4% (Table 10 ), and the within-visitor shift appears in each campaign ( + 1.46 +1.46 points for the men’s and + 0.44 +0.44 for the women’s). Adjusting for the covariates (recency, history, mens, womens, newbie, and the channel and zip-code dummies) in a logistic regression among the 9,394 visitors, with HC1 standard errors, gives a treatment coefficient of + 0.186 +0.186 (SE 0.105 0.105 , p = 0.076 p=0.076 , odds ratio 1.20 1.20 ) and an average marginal effect of + 1.03 +1.03 points (SE 0.55 0.55 points, p = 0.064 p=0.064 ). The violation survives conditioning on X X with its size intact but is not significant at conventional levels, so Hillstrom suggests conditional-mean noninvariance rather than establishing it; Criteo establishes it (Section 5.2 ). The estimator behavior is not in doubt: a prediction model trained on pooled labeled data estimates a single 𝔼 ⁡ [ Y | S = 1 ] \mathbb{E}[Y|S=1] and underestimates conversion among treated visitors, an estimator problem that PPI++ repairs, unlike the estimand problem of converter-only metrics (Section 2.1 ). This is the local-alternative regime of Proposition 7 : when T n T_{n} is small relative to c c , the weight stays near one, the hybrid keeps part of the SI bias, and its interval carries no guarantee (Remark 4 ). On Hillstrom, PPI++ is the analysis to report, and the hybrid is at most a display of estimator disagreement.

sections.heading: 5.2 Criteo: the same funnel violation at industrial scale
sections.text: The Criteo uplift data ( Diemert et al., 2018 ) , released by Criteo AI Lab, come from a randomized advertising experiment; the v2.1 release has 13,979,592 users (treatment n 1 = 11,882,655 n_{1}=11{,}882{,}655 ; control n 0 = 2,096,937 n_{0}=2{,}096{,}937 ), twelve anonymized covariates, a visit indicator (the surrogate), and a conversion indicator (the outcome). The funnel replicates Hillstrom’s at 218 times the scale: no user converts without visiting, visits are roughly sixteen times as common as conversions, and treatment raises the visit rate from 3.82% to 4.85%, the conversion rate from 0.194% to 0.309% (masking target 0.00115 0.00115 ), and the conversion rate among visitors from 5.07% to 6.36%, an unadjusted within-visitor conditional-mean difference of + 1.29 +1.29 points. A logistic regression of conversion on treatment and the covariates f 0 f_{0} through f 11 f_{11} among the 656,929 visitors, with HC1 standard errors, gives a treatment coefficient of + 0.310 +0.310 (SE 0.020 0.020 , p < 10 − 16 p<10^{-16} , odds ratio 1.36 1.36 ) and a covariate-adjusted within-visitor difference of + 1.35 +1.35 points (SE 0.08 0.08 points, p < 10 − 16 p<10^{-16} ). That is a decisive rejection within one fitted specification, not a model-free verification that conditional-mean invariance fails: another specification of the visitor-level model could in principle absorb the coefficient. Two independent advertising-response funnels thus show the same within-funnel pattern at similar magnitude; other funnel types (signup, activation, trial-to-paid) remain untested. The two adjusted violations are nearly the same size, + 1.35 +1.35 points at Criteo and + 1.03 +1.03 at Hillstrom, but only one is statistically visible: p < 10 − 16 p<10^{-16} at n = 14 n=14 million against p = 0.064 p=0.064 at n = 64,000 n=64{,}000 . Damage before detection applies to the evidence for the violation as well as to the diagnostic meant to catch it. At this scale the violation is both fatal to the surrogate index and detected. Subsampling traces the transition (Table 12 ). The SI bias is nearly scale-invariant, − 5.1 -5.1 to − 5.7 × 10 − 4 -5.7\times 10^{-4} ( − 44 % -44\% to − 50 % -50\% relative), as expected of a structural violation, while SI coverage falls from 0.847 0.847 at n = 10,000 n=10{,}000 to 0.660 0.660 at 30,000 30{,}000 , 0.183 0.183 at 100,000 100{,}000 , and zero from 300,000 300{,}000 on. The diagnostic’s rejection rate is flat between 0.197 0.197 and 0.270 0.270 through n = 300,000 n=300{,}000 , a spread of about two Monte Carlo standard errors, crosses majority detection only around n ≈ 10 6 n\approx 10^{6} , and saturates by n = 3 n=3 million. Between roughly 10 4 10^{4} and 10 6 10^{6} lies the real-data detection-damage gap: two orders of magnitude of sample size across which SI inference is invalid and the diagnostic is usually silent (Figure 7 ). Hillstrom shows the same pattern at n = 64,000 n=64{,}000 , with 7.2% SI coverage and an 11% rejection rate; its effect size, conversion rate, and variances differ from Criteo’s. The same table carries the clearest counterexample to PPI++’s own validity: its exact-variance coverage is 0.850 0.850 at n = 30,000 n=30{,}000 and 0.897 0.897 at n = 10,000 n=10{,}000 , both outside their bands (the ordering of the two is within Monte Carlo error). The mechanism is outcome rarity, not label scarcity. With conversions near two in a thousand and an 85/15 treatment–control split, a subsample’s labeled control arm holds a handful of conversions, the arm means are far from normal, and the Wald interval PPI++ inherits from the labeled-only estimator undercovers although the exact variance is in use. DGP 5 varies how many Gaussian outcomes are observed, so the simulations do not cover this regime.

sections.heading: 5.3 A Criteo-calibrated semi-synthetic testbed
sections.text: The DGPs of Section 3 are stylized, and the Hillstrom and Criteo analyses are single realizations with violations of fixed size. A semi-synthetic testbed bridges the two. We fit logistic models for the two stages of the Criteo funnel (visit given covariates and treatment; conversion given a visit, covariates, and treatment), resample covariate rows from the real data, and keep conversion impossible without a visit. The fitted within-funnel treatment coefficient, κ ^ = 0.31 \hat{\kappa}=0.31 , is placed on a dial in units of the observed violation: dial 0 imposes conditional-mean invariance exactly, dial 1 reproduces Criteo’s violation, and dial 2 doubles it, with covariates, funnel rates, and outcome sparsity held at their calibrated values. We run the standard protocol at the Hillstrom scale ( n = 64,000 n=64{,}000 , π L = 0.20 \pi_{L}=0.20 , OLS prediction model, R = 500 R=500 per dial), measuring bias and coverage against the known simulated τ \tau of each dial. Table 13 reports the sweep. At dial 0 the calibrated funnel behaves like DGP 1: SI is nearly unbiased with large gains (RE 5.7 × 5.7\times ) and mild over-coverage at 0.976 0.976 , PPI++ delivers RE 1.06 1.06 at 0.942 0.942 coverage, and the diagnostic rejects at its nominal size (6.2%). The residual SI relative bias at dial 0 ( + 3.5 % +3.5\% ) is within 1.4 Monte Carlo standard errors of zero; to the extent it is real, the OLS model’s inability to represent the logistic conversion surface is the natural source, since surrogacy holds by construction. At this tiny τ \tau the relative biases of the noisier estimators carry Monte Carlo standard errors of roughly ± 14 \pm 14 percentage points, so the single-digit LO and PPI++ entries of Table A11 are indistinguishable from zero. At dial 1, the violation the real data exhibit, SI coverage collapses to 8% at − 68 % -68\% relative bias while the diagnostic detects the violation on only 10% of replications, close to the Hillstrom rejection rate (11%) at the same sample size; the testbed is calibrated to Criteo, not Hillstrom, so the agreement reflects similar violation-to-noise ratios rather than a fitted correspondence. At twice the real violation, detection reaches only 35% while SI coverage is exactly zero, and PPI++ is unbiased with near-nominal coverage at every dial. We add a post-treatment engagement proxy and split the fitted conversion-stage violation between it and a residual direct effect. sections.heading: 5.4 LaLonde: a negative control with a pre-treatment “surrogate”
sections.text: The LaLonde National Supported Work (NSW) experiment ( LaLonde, 1986 ) randomized 445 individuals into a job-training program (treatment, n 1 = 185 n_{1}=185 ) or control ( n 0 = 260 n_{0}=260 ). We treat 1975 earnings (RE75) as the “surrogate” and 1978 earnings (RE78) as the outcome; the masking target is $ 1,794 \$1{,}794 , and the results over R = 500 R=500 random splits are in the replication package. RE75 was realized before the 1976–1977 program began, so treatment cannot have caused it, and it fails the Prentice requirement that the surrogate lie on the causal path. As the simulations predict, the surrogate index is massively biased: at π L = 0.20 \pi_{L}=0.20 its bias is − $ 1,645 -\$1{,}645 ( − 92 % -92\% ) with 5.2% coverage, and at π L = 0.50 \pi_{L}=0.50 its coverage is 0%. PPI++ keeps near-zero bias and 92.6–98.8% coverage at π L ∈ { 0.10 , 0.20 , 0.50 } \pi_{L}\in\{0.10,0.20,0.50\} , reverting to the labeled-only baseline (RE 0.99 0.99 – 1.00 1.00 ); the 92.6% at π L = 0.10 \pi_{L}=0.10 reflects the small labeled sample ( n L ≈ 45 n_{L}\approx 45 ). The diagnostic rejects on 11.8%, 15.2%, and 36.8% of splits at the three labeled fractions, the limited power available at n = 445 n=445 : in small samples, domain knowledge must drive surrogate selection.

sections.heading: 6 Practical Recommendations
sections.text: The workflow below separates a prespecified primary inferential analysis from sensitivity analyses and decision exploration. Its thresholds are calibrated to our DGPs and should be adapted to a platform’s context.

sections.heading: The principle.
sections.text: Prespecify the primary inferential analysis before reading the experiment. Under MCAR labeling and adequate labeled outcome counts in each arm, PPI++ with the exact tuning constant of Equation ( 13 ) and the exact variance of Proposition 5 is the default primary analysis when surrogacy is uncertain. The surrogate index and the hybrid are sensitivity analyses or tools for decision exploration. A team that wants the surrogate index as its primary analysis must justify surrogacy independently of the diagnostic, from prior validation studies or a mechanism by which treatment cannot bypass the surrogate, and should record that justification before the data are read. A data-adaptive rule that selects the interval after the diagnostic would need validation of the whole selection procedure, which we do not provide.

sections.heading: Step 0: Establish that the workflow applies.
sections.text: Three conditions need separate justification before the steps below. Labeling: the PPI++ guarantee is an MCAR guarantee. Under nonrandom labeling unadjusted PPI++ has no design-based centering (under mix drift in DGP 11 it carries − 5.0 % -5.0\% relative bias and its exact variance estimator underestimates the sampling variance), and an estimator that models the labeling, such as AIPW with a correct observation model, is needed. Enrollment-effect drift: under the calendar interpretation the labeled units are the earliest enrollees. Compare the ( X i , S i ) (X_{i},S_{i}) distributions and the treatment effect on the surrogate across enrollment waves; covariate-mix drift is repairable by reweighting on observables, and the model-based estimators tolerate it (Section 4.4 ). Covariate checks cannot establish that the treatment effect on the outcome is stable, however, and drift in that effect is not repairable: every estimator we test carries roughly a third of the effect as bias at g e = 0.2 g_{e}=0.2 . If effect drift is plausible, report the review as an early read on the early cohort, not as an estimate of the eventual effect. Sparse outcomes: count labeled outcome events in each arm, not the total sample. At the n = 30,000 n=30{,}000 Criteo subsample PPI++ covers 0.850 0.850 because the labeled control arm holds only a handful of conversions (Section 5.2 ); sparse outcomes need separately justified inference or more labels. A prediction model trained on a separate prior cohort (Regime B) adds a transport assumption that DGP 4 shows can fail, and its estimates are exploratory until transport is verified.

sections.heading: Step 1: The primary analysis.
sections.text: Fit f ^ \hat{f} on the labeled units under all-units cross-fitting and compute PPI++ with the common, unclipped coefficient of Equation ( 13 ); in the e-commerce example f ^ \hat{f} maps funnel signals to conversion on the early enrollees whose conversion windows have closed. Form the interval from V ^ corrected = V ^ plug ​ - ​ in + ∑ t 2 ​ λ ^ ​ ( γ ^ t − λ ^ ​ σ ^ Y ^ , t 2 ) / n t \hat{V}_{\mathrm{corrected}}=\hat{V}_{\mathrm{plug\text{-}in}}+\sum_{t}2\hat{\lambda}(\hat{\gamma}_{t}-\hat{\lambda}\hat{\sigma}^{2}_{\hat{Y},t})/n_{t} at that coefficient, so that the interval and the tuning rule come from one objective. The overlap correction is largest when the coefficient sits below the per-arm optimum, as under a plug-in rule or a binding clip, and matters most at π L > 0.30 \pi_{L}>0.30 ; at the exact coefficient it is small when the arms have similar labeled fractions, and it is computed in every case. The population-optimal coefficient gives a variance no larger than labeled-only’s (Proposition 4 ), but an estimated coefficient carries no finite-sample guarantee; in our designs RE is 1.4 1.4 – 1.5 × 1.5\times at π L ≤ 0.20 \pi_{L}\leq 0.20 and falls toward 1.0 × 1.0\times as π L \pi_{L} approaches one.

sections.heading: Step 2: Read the diagnostic as a warning.
sections.text: Compute τ ^ SI \hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{SI}} and the two-sided estimator-disagreement statistic of Section 2.5 . We suggest α = 0.10 \alpha=0.10 , a heuristic that favors detection because an undetected violation usually costs more than a false alarm. A rejection is evidence that the two estimands diverge, through a surrogacy failure or prediction-model misspecification, and the surrogate index and the hybrid should then not inform the decision. A non-rejection neither establishes surrogacy nor licenses the SI interval: reporting the nominal SI interval after a non-rejection is the hard-switch rule of Table A4 , whose coverage in DGP 2 is 0.699 0.699 at ρ = 0.2 \rho=0.2 and 0.706 0.706 at ρ = 0.4 \rho=0.4 . Power is also low where it matters: under DGP 2 at n = 10,000 n=10{,}000 and π L = 0.20 \pi_{L}=0.20 the test at α = 0.10 \alpha=0.10 detects ρ = 0.2 \rho=0.2 on 19.2% of replications (Section 4.3 ); at n = 100,000 n=100{,}000 power at α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 reaches 79%, and at n = 1,000 n=1{,}000 it is negligible (Table A6 ).

sections.heading: Step 3: Sensitivity analysis and decision exploration.
sections.text: Report the surrogate index beside the primary analysis as a sensitivity analysis. Under valid surrogacy it is far more precise, with RE 5.5 × 5.5\times at π L = 0.05 \pi_{L}=0.05 and 2.9 × 2.9\times at π L = 0.20 \pi_{L}=0.20 (Table 4 ), the gain available when the surrogacy assumption is independently justified. The hybrid with c = 1.5 c=1.5 can be reported as an exploratory point estimate (RE 1.5 1.5 – 2.2 × 2.2\times under valid surrogacy); its interval has no coverage guarantee at fixed c c (Remark 4 ), and when its mean weight on SI exceeds about 0.5 0.5 while a direct effect is plausible, it carries much of any undetected SI bias, as on Hillstrom (10.7% relative bias at mean weight 0.64 0.64 ).

sections.heading: Step 4: Separate formal inference from portfolio launch triage.
sections.text: Formal inference rests on the primary analysis of Step 1. For go-or-no-go launch triage, biased surrogate estimators can still achieve high correct-decision rates when the surrogate preserves the sign of the effect, and in the valid-surrogacy portfolio of DGP 6 the naive surrogate and the surrogate index attain the lowest regret (Section 4.5 ). That ranking depends on the objective: DGP 6 charges effect-size-weighted loss with no launch cost, so a platform whose launches carry real costs, or whose candidates include harmful changes, should re-derive the triage rule under its own objective.

sections.heading: 7 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.text: The central finding is a sharp robustness–efficiency tradeoff among surrogate estimators. Surrogate-based methods deliver large efficiency gains when surrogacy holds and lose coverage under moderate violations, while PPI-family methods stay asymptotically valid under MCAR labeling with adequate labeled outcome counts in each arm, at modest gains (Section 4 ). On the calendar, the week-2.5 PPI++ interval matches labeled-only at about week 2.97, so PPI++ shortens the wait by roughly half a week without imposing surrogacy, while a valid surrogate index at the same review is already narrower than labeled-only at full maturation in week six, a saving of three and a half weeks; which of those claims a team will stake a launch on is the robustness–efficiency choice. Diagnostics help but do not validate surrogacy: under partial mediation some coverage-destroying violations are statistically invisible at both sample sizes we examine (Section 4.3 ), and the exploratory hybrid mitigates that risk without removing it. Enrollment-time labeling is benign without drift and survivable under covariate-mix drift, but drift in the treatment effect breaks every estimator (Section 4.4 ), so reading the review date as a choice of π L \pi_{L} requires effect stability over the enrollment window. These conclusions have several limitations. We test two prediction model classes (OLS and GBT); neural networks or heavily tuned ensembles could change the efficiency profiles, though the SI bias is structural rather than model-driven. Apart from DGP 3’s group heterogeneity and the covariate-heterogeneous surrogate effect behind DGP 11’s mix drift, the DGPs have constant treatment effects, and a surrogate valid for the ATE may be invalid for conditional effects, which leaves surrogate-based heterogeneous-effect estimation open. The hybrid’s c = 1.5 c=1.5 rests on the finite-sample grids and the limit experiment, and the covariance-adaptive rule of Table A2 matches it on the cells tested, but covariance structures far from ours are untested. The diagnostic has limited power at n < 1,000 n<1{,}000 and at moderate violations ( ρ ≤ 0.2 \rho\leq 0.2 at n = 10,000 n=10{,}000 ). The composite proxy’s weights come from one simulated library of past experiments per run, drawn from the same DGP family as the current experiment, so its results are optimistic relative to practice and do not average over library estimation uncertainty. Rare outcomes bound the main recommendation: at the sparse Criteo subsamples PPI++ covers 0.850 0.850 and 0.897 0.897 (Table 12 ) because the normal approximation for the labeled arm means fails, a regime our simulations do not cover and for which we evaluate no sparse-event method. Finally, the real-data analyses use binary funnel surrogates; the calibrated multi-surrogate experiment (Table 14 ) shows that enriching the index removes roughly the share of the violation the added signals mediate, but validation on real multi-metric indices, continuous engagement surrogates, revenue outcomes, and proprietary platform data remains for future work. These findings connect to recent theory. Ji et al. (2025) unify the surrogate index and PPI as endpoints of a bias–variance spectrum, and our simulations characterize that spectrum in finite samples under realistic failure modes. Mozer (2026) shows that PPI++ is the classical difference estimator of Cassel et al. (1976) , and survey-sampling experience favors such model-assisted estimators when auxiliary information is unreliable, the conclusion our simulations reach. Kallus and Mao (2025) derive the semiparametric efficiency bound for treatment effects with limited outcome data in a missing-data model that does not impose statistical surrogacy, and construct estimators that attain it; that bound concerns their model, not the surrogacy-imposing one in which the surrogate index gains its efficiency, and we do not benchmark against it. Our corrected variance (Proposition 5 ) writes the exact fixed-predictor variance of PPI++ in the all-units parameterization, the form in which practitioners most often implement it and in which the overlap covariance is easiest to lose; it agrees with the variance the labeled-unlabeled form of Angelopoulos et al. (2023b) assigns after the change of tuning variable. Several extensions are open: a sequential hybrid that updates c c as data accumulate, paired with anytime-valid inference ( Kilian et al., 2025 ) to monitor the weight w w during an experiment; a Bayesian formulation with a prior on the violation ρ \rho that encodes domain knowledge about surrogate reliability; and a formal account of combining CUPED with PPI++, which exploit pre- and post-treatment information respectively and are routinely applied together. For a team deciding at a mid-experiment review whether to call the result, the message is to prespecify PPI++ with the exact variance as the primary analysis when the conditions of Section 6 hold, to read the diagnostic as a warning, and to report the surrogate index as a sensitivity analysis. The workflow requires no additional data collection and adds negligible computational cost.

sections.heading: Appendix A The Adaptive Hybrid Estimator
sections.text: This appendix gives the hybrid’s construction, the risk analysis that fixes its tuning constant, the simulation grids behind Section 4.8 , and the asymptotics of a diverging- c n c_{n} variant.

sections.heading: A.1 Construction and Interval
sections.text: A hard-switch rule would choose between SI and PPI++; the exploratory hybrid instead combines them continuously, interpolating between the two according to the evidence against surrogacy. It belongs to the frequentist model-averaging family of Hjort and Claeskens (2003) (see also Claeskens and Hjort, 2008 ), a compromise estimator whose data-dependent weight is a smooth function of a specification statistic, and it inherits that family’s risk behavior, including the raw-risk hump at intermediate violations characteristic of pretest and shrinkage estimators ( Judge and Bock, 1978 ) , which Proposition 7 characterizes exactly for our weight.

sections.heading: Definition.
sections.text: The adaptive hybrid estimator is τ ^ hybrid = w ⋅ τ ^ SI + ( 1 − w ) ⋅ τ ^ PPI + + , \hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{hybrid}}=w\cdot\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{SI}}+(1-w)\cdot\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{PPI++}}, (39) where the Cauchy-kernel weight w = c c + T n 2 w=\frac{c}{c+T_{n}^{2}} (40) smoothly transitions from w ≈ 1 w\approx 1 (use SI) when T n ≈ 0 T_{n}\approx 0 to w ≈ 0 w\approx 0 (use PPI++) when | T n | |T_{n}| is large. We recommend c = 1.5 c=1.5 based on the minimax analysis of Section A.3 . Two versions must be kept apart. The fixed- c c hybrid, run everywhere in this paper, holds c c constant and is characterized exactly by the limit experiment below. A diverging- c n c_{n} variant has cleaner asymptotic endpoints: with c n → ∞ c_{n}\to\infty it attains the surrogate index’s asymptotic variance under H 0 H_{0} , and with c n = o ⁡ ( n ) c_{n}=o(\sqrt{n}) it is root- n n equivalent to PPI++ under a fixed violation (Propositions 8 and 9 , Section A.6 ). Under local alternatives δ n = h / n \delta_{n}=h/\sqrt{n} , however, the diagnostic statistic stays O p ​ ( 1 ) O_{p}(1) , so c n → ∞ c_{n}\to\infty forces w → 1 w\to 1 and the diverging- c n c_{n} hybrid inherits SI’s local bias in full; the nondegenerate weight limit that makes the hybrid interesting under local alternatives belongs to the fixed- c c version. We therefore claim no uniform oracle bound for either, and justify c = 1.5 c=1.5 by the limit experiment and the minimax grids of Section A.3 . The data-dependent weight w w invalidates the standard Wald CI, so we construct a simulation-calibrated CI as follows. The 2 × 2 2\times 2 covariance matrix of ( τ ^ SI , τ ^ PPI + + ) (\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{SI}},\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{PPI++}}) is Σ ^ = Ω ^ / n \hat{\Sigma}=\hat{\Omega}/n , the sandwich of Proposition 3 ; the same Σ ^ \hat{\Sigma} supplies SE ⁡ ( D ^ ) \mathrm{SE}(\hat{D}) , so the weight and the interval are built from one covariance estimate. We then draw M = 10,000 M=10{,}000 samples from 𝒩 ⁡ ( ( τ ^ SI , τ ^ PPI + + ) T , Σ ^ ) \mathcal{N}\bigl((\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{SI}},\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{PPI++}})^{T},\hat{\Sigma}\bigr) ; on each draw we compute T n ( m ) T_{n}^{(m)} , w ( m ) w^{(m)} , and τ ^ hybrid ( m ) \hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{hybrid}}^{(m)} , and report the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles as the 95% CI. The construction parallels the smoothed post-model-averaging intervals of Efron (2014) . Remark 4 (The simulation-calibrated interval is a heuristic, not a consistent procedure) . We make no consistency claim for this interval at fixed c c . For fixed c c the hybrid is a non-regular shrinkage estimator: its weight is a fixed smooth function of T n T_{n} , and the standardized gap h / σ D h/\sigma_{D} that determines the weight’s limiting distribution is estimated with error that does not vanish at the n \sqrt{n} scale on which the weight operates. The plug-in percentile distribution therefore fails to converge to the sampling distribution of the hybrid. This is the shrinkage-estimator instance of the general failure of resampling and plug-in distributional approximations near a pretest null ( Leeb and Pötscher, 2005 ) . Under fixed detectable violations, w → 𝑝 0 w\xrightarrow{p}0 and the interval inherits PPI++ validity: it collapses onto the exact-variance PPI++ interval, which is valid under Assumption 1 and the regularity conditions of Proposition 3 . We report the interval’s coverage empirically rather than claiming it: 94–96% under valid surrogacy across the tested configurations, 93.1–93.4% at ρ ∈ { 0.2 , 0.4 } \rho\in\{0.2,0.4\} , and 93.0% on Hillstrom at π L = 0.20 \pi_{L}=0.20 (Sections A.4 and 5 ). The hybrid is an exploratory estimator, and its interval should be read as a display of estimator disagreement rather than as formal inference.

The objective is flat near its optimum: over ± 0.2 \pm 0.2 around c ∗ c^{*} the worst-case excess varies by 11.5% and 13.4%, and the five best values of c c are { 1.4 , … , 1.8 } \{1.4,\ldots,1.8\} and { 1.1 , … , 1.5 } \{1.1,\ldots,1.5\} , so c = 1.5 c=1.5 is in both windows. sections.heading: A.4 Hybrid Simulation Results
sections.text: The canonical hybrid run is the R = 2,000 R=2{,}000 evaluation on DGPs 1, 2, and 9 (replication package). Under valid surrogacy (DGP 1) the hybrid delivers RE 2.0 2.0 – 2.2 × 2.2\times over labeled-only at π L = 0.05 \pi_{L}=0.05 – 0.20 0.20 , falling to 1.5 × 1.5\times at π L = 0.50 \pi_{L}=0.50 , with 94–96% coverage; DGP 2 at ρ = 0 \rho=0 , the same model on independent draws, gives 1.9 1.9 – 2.3 × 2.3\times . The average weight is about 0.7 0.7 . Adaptivity has a finite-sample cost: the hybrid does not reach the surrogate index’s own efficiency ( 5.54 × 5.54\times at π L = 0.05 \pi_{L}=0.05 and 2.91 × 2.91\times at π L = 0.20 \pi_{L}=0.20 , Table 4 ), because it hedges against a violation. Under moderate violation (DGP 2 at π L = 0.20 \pi_{L}=0.20 ) the average weight falls from 0.63 at ρ = 0.2 \rho=0.2 to 0.30 at ρ = 0.4 \rho=0.4 as T n T_{n} grows. The hybrid retains part of the SI bias (relative bias − 8.4 % -8.4\% and − 9.0 % -9.0\% ) with coverage of 93.1–93.4%, far above SI’s but below nominal. At ρ = 0.2 \rho=0.2 it still has the lowest RMSE of the three estimators; by ρ = 0.4 \rho=0.4 PPI++ dominates it (RMSE 0.050 against 0.056), the raw-risk hump of Proposition 7 appearing in finite samples. Under antagonistic surrogacy (DGP 9) the weight is near zero in every replication (mean 0.012 0.012 at π L = 0.20 \pi_{L}=0.20 ), so the hybrid reverts to PPI++ and avoids SI’s wrong-sign estimate. These results describe the detectable-violation regime; Hillstrom illustrates the undetectable one (Section 5.1 ). The coverage figures are reported, not guaranteed (Remark 4 ). Against a nonparametric alternative, the simulation-calibrated interval does at least as well at a fraction of the cost. On DGP 1 at π L = 0.20 \pi_{L}=0.20 it covers 96.2% of replications and a percentile bootstrap with B = 200 B=200 covers 95.0%, with mean widths 0.163 0.163 and 0.160 0.160 ; on DGP 2 at ρ = 0.2 \rho=0.2 the two cover 93.2% and 92.4%, with widths 0.170 0.170 and 0.167 0.167 ( R = 500 R=500 , M = 10,000 M=10{,}000 , c = 1.5 c=1.5 ). Both under-cover in the violation cell, and the comparison does not isolate the cause. The featured violation cell (DGP 2, ρ = 0.2 \rho=0.2 , π L = 0.20 \pi_{L}=0.20 ) appears in several runs. Hybrid coverage is 0.934 0.934 in the canonical evaluation and in the hard-switch comparison (Table A4 ), 0.952 0.952 on the R = 1,000 R=1{,}000 sensitivity grid (Table A3 ), and 0.932 0.932 in the R = 500 R=500 interval validation. SI coverage is 0.682 0.682 in Table 6 , 0.680 0.680 in the paired run of Section 4.3 , 0.654 0.654 in Table A4 , and 0.638 0.638 in Table A12 . Within each estimator, no two values differ by more than about two Monte Carlo standard errors of the difference, and the text quotes the canonical runs.

sections.heading: A.5 Sensitivity in c c and the Hard-Switch Comparison
sections.text: The sensitivity analysis (Table A3 ) confirms that c = 1.5 c=1.5 balances efficiency under valid surrogacy ( 1.95 × 1.95\times RE) against coverage under violations ( 95.2 % 95.2\% at ρ = 0.2 \rho=0.2 and 92.9 % 92.9\% at ρ = 0.4 \rho=0.4 on the sensitivity grid). A comparison with the naive hard-switch strategy (Table A4 ) shows the switch suffers from pre-test bias: its coverage drops to 69.9% at ρ = 0.2 \rho=0.2 and 70.6% at ρ = 0.4 \rho=0.4 , while the hybrid holds 93.4% and 93.1% in the same cells. sections.heading: B.2 Proof of Proposition 2 (Unbiasedness of PPI at a Fixed Predictor)
sections.text: Proof. Condition on the treatment vector and on the labeled counts n L , t ≥ 1 n_{L,t}\geq 1 . Because T T is independent of the potential outcomes and the units are i.i.d., the units of arm t t are an i.i.d. sample from the distribution of ( X , S ⁡ ( t ) , Y ⁡ ( t ) ) (X,S(t),Y(t)) , and Y ^ i = f ⁡ ( S i , X i ) \hat{Y}_{i}=f(S_{i},X_{i}) is a fixed function of each unit’s own data. Under Assumption 1 the labeled units of arm t t are a simple random subset of that arm of size n L , t n_{L,t} , drawn independently of the units’ data. A simple random subset has the same expected mean as the set it is drawn from, so 𝔼 ⁡ [ Y ¯ L , t ] = 𝔼 ⁡ [ Y ⁡ ( t ) ] , 𝔼 ⁡ [ Y ^ ¯ L , t ] = 𝔼 ⁡ [ Y ^ ¯ t ] . \mathbb{E}\bigl[\bar{Y}_{L,t}\bigr]=\mathbb{E}[Y(t)],\qquad\mathbb{E}\bigl[\bar{\hat{Y}}_{L,t}\bigr]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\bar{\hat{Y}}_{t}\bigr]. The first identity gives 𝔼 ⁡ [ τ ^ Y ℒ ] = 𝔼 ⁡ [ Y ⁡ ( 1 ) ] − 𝔼 ⁡ [ Y ⁡ ( 0 ) ] = τ \mathbb{E}[\hat{\tau}_{Y}^{\mathcal{L}}]=\mathbb{E}[Y(1)]-\mathbb{E}[Y(0)]=\tau , and the second, differenced across arms, gives 𝔼 ⁡ [ τ ^ Y ^ all − τ ^ Y ^ ℒ ] = 0 \mathbb{E}[\hat{\tau}_{\hat{Y}}^{\mathrm{all}}-\hat{\tau}_{\hat{Y}}^{\mathcal{L}}]=0 . For the fold-level statement, fix fold k k and condition on the fold assignment, the treatment vector, β ^ ( − k ) \hat{\beta}_{(-k)} , and the labeled count n L , t ​ k n_{L,tk} of fold k k in each arm. The fit β ^ ( − k ) \hat{\beta}_{(-k)} is a function of the data and labels of units outside fold k k only. The units of fold k k are independent of those, and under Assumption 1 their labels, given n L , t ​ k n_{L,tk} , form a simple random subset of the fold’s units in arm t t whatever the labels outside the fold. Every unit of fold k k is scored by the coefficient β ^ ( − k ) \hat{\beta}_{(-k)} , which is fixed under this conditioning, so the argument above applies within the fold and the fold’s labeled mean of Y ^ \hat{Y} in arm t t has the conditional expectation of its all-units mean. ∎

sections.heading: C.3 Hybrid Risk by Regime
sections.text: We claim neither a uniform-oracle MSE bound for the hybrid nor consistency of its plug-in interval (Remark 4 ). Proposition 7 is the operative result; the two paragraphs below record the endpoints it interpolates between. Fixed detectable alternatives. If | δ | / SE ⁡ ( D ^ ) → ∞ |\delta|/\mathrm{SE}(\hat{D})\to\infty then T n 2 → ∞ T_{n}^{2}\to\infty in probability and w → 𝑝 0 w\xrightarrow{p}0 , so the hybrid converges to PPI++ and the interval collapses onto the exact-variance PPI++ interval. The interval inherits PPI validity in this regime, under Assumption 1 and the regularity conditions of Proposition 3 . Local alternatives. Along δ n \delta_{n} with n ​ 𝔼 ​ [ D ^ ] → h \sqrt{n}\,\mathbb{E}[\hat{D}]\to h , the statistic T n T_{n} converges in distribution to 𝒩 ⁡ ( h / σ D , 1 ) \mathcal{N}(h/\sigma_{D},1) , so w w converges in distribution to a non-degenerate random variable in ( 0 , 1 ) (0,1) and the hybrid is a random convex combination of SI and PPI++. The expected MSE involves the distribution of w w times the SI bias, which is non-zero and does not vanish; Proposition 7 characterizes this regime exactly. This is the regime in which the Hillstrom hybrid carries 10.7% relative bias, and it is also the regime in which the plug-in interval has no coverage guarantee: the standardized gap h / σ D h/\sigma_{D} is estimated with error that stays O p ​ ( 1 ) O_{p}(1) at exactly the scale on which the weight varies, so the simulated percentile distribution does not converge to the hybrid’s sampling distribution ( Leeb and Pötscher, 2005 ) . We therefore present the fixed- c c hybrid as an exploratory shrinkage estimator with an exact limit-experiment risk characterization and an empirically reported interval, not as a theorem-backed inferential procedure. The fixed c = 1.5 c=1.5 is justified by the limit-experiment and finite-sample minimax analyses of Appendix A , not by an MSE oracle bound.

sections.heading: F.3 Ablations and Variance Checks
sections.text: Every ablation configuration runs inside the same replication as the primary one, on the same draws and fitted predictions, so the tables below are paired cell by cell with the main-text tables and their row differences carry much less Monte Carlo error than a comparison of independent runs, though pairing does not remove it. The PPI++ ablations use the plug-in tuning rule, the plug-in variance, a clipped coefficient, a per-arm coefficient, or the plug-in rule and plug-in variance together (the plug-in-rule estimator end to end); the surrogate-index ablations use the plug-in and the delta-method first-stage variances. This subsection also holds the variance checks behind Section 2.5 .

In the linear designs only the plug-in tuning rule moves anything material: it sits below the per-arm optimum by the factor 1 / ( 1 + π L ) 1/(1+\pi_{L}) , so RE falls from 1.524 1.524 to 1.519 1.519 at π L = 0.05 \pi_{L}=0.05 , from 1.395 1.395 to 1.376 1.376 at π L = 0.20 \pi_{L}=0.20 , and from 1.185 1.185 to 1.158 1.158 at π L = 0.50 \pi_{L}=0.50 , a loss of 0.3 % 0.3\% , 1.4 % 1.4\% , and 2.3 % 2.3\% , with intervals 0.1 % 0.1\% to 2.3 % 2.3\% wider. sections.heading: Variance checks outside Proposition 3 .
sections.text: Two of the three designs the proposition does not cover (Table 3 ) are checked on two cells each. For the gradient-boosted-tree rows, which use the fixed-predictor plug-in variance and covariance, the check runs DGP 1 with π L = 0.20 \pi_{L}=0.20 and DGP 2 with ρ = 0.2 \rho=0.2 on the GBT comparison’s own draws ( R = 200 R=200 , with a paired bootstrap of B = 100 B=100 draws that refit the trees). The plug-in variance is 0.95 0.95 (Monte Carlo standard error 0.11 0.11 ) and 1.13 1.13 ( 0.11 0.11 ) of the Monte Carlo variance of τ ^ SI \hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{SI}} , within Monte Carlo error of one on these two cells and silent about other designs; surrogate-index coverage is 0.940 0.940 at DGP 1 and 0.665 0.665 at DGP 2, where the shortfall is the − 0.039 -0.039 bias. The fixed-predictor Var ⁡ ( D ^ ) \mathrm{Var}(\hat{D}) is 1.07 1.07 ( 0.11 0.11 ) and 0.94 0.94 ( 0.10 0.10 ) of the Monte Carlo variance, and the diagnostic’s size at DGP 1 is 0.065 0.065 ( 0.017 0.017 ) at α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 and 0.105 0.105 ( 0.022 0.022 ) at α = 0.10 \alpha=0.10 . A bootstrap that assigns folds to resampled rows lets copies of one unit fall on both sides of a fold, where trees partly memorize them, and understates Var ⁡ ( τ ^ PPI + + ) \mathrm{Var}(\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{PPI++}}) at 0.74 0.74 and 0.79 0.79 and Var ⁡ ( D ^ ) \mathrm{Var}(\hat{D}) at 0.67 0.67 and 0.60 0.60 of the Monte Carlo variance. With clustered folds the tree bootstrap is a validation reference on this one cell, and it agrees with the direct check. For the MAR and enrollment-drift rows, which apply the MCAR sandwich with the labeled-design Q ^ \hat{Q} , the check runs DGP 5 MAR with q = 0.10 q=0.10 and DGP 11 mix drift with d = 2 d=2 at R = 500 R=500 , with a paired bootstrap of B = 200 B=200 draws that resamples units within arm with their labels. sections.heading: The joint covariance.
sections.text: Tables A19 and A20 are the calibration checks summarized in Section 2.5 . The joint paired bootstrap resamples units with replacement stratified by arm, keeps every copy of a resampled unit in its unit’s fold, refits the index on the resampled labeled units under the all-units protocol, and recomputes both estimators, so it carries every source of first-stage uncertainty. A Finite-Sample Comparison Under Realistic Failure Modes Zihao Chen Affiliation: University of Washington Email: zchen05@uw.edu September 2026 Abstract Online experiments must often be evaluated before long-term outcomes mature. Under rolling enrollment, these outcomes are observed only for early enrollees, while short-term surrogates are available for everyone. We compare seven estimators across eleven data-generating processes, spanning partial mediation, drift, outcome sparsity, and enrollment-time labeling, with up to R = 2,000 R=2{,}000 replications over more than 500 method-by-scenario cells. We find a sharp robustness–efficiency tradeoff: the surrogate index delivers large efficiency gains when surrogacy holds but its coverage collapses under violations, while PPI-family methods stay asymptotically valid under random labeling at smaller gains. We give the finite-sample variance of PPI++ in the all-units parameterization for a fixed predictor, a joint asymptotic distribution for the two estimators under cross-fitting, and a Hausman-type estimator-disagreement diagnostic, then quantify the detection-damage gap: in the partial-mediation design, where we locate both edges, a band of violations destroys surrogate-index coverage yet is too small to detect on most datasets. On the 64,000-customer Hillstrom experiment the diagnostic rarely flags a violation that biases the surrogate index, and a Cauchy-kernel hybrid of the two estimators inherits 10.7% relative bias; on the 14-million-user Criteo experiment the violation is detected, and subsampling traces detection turning on with scale as damage persists. PPI++ has limits: at a rare-conversion n = 30,000 n=30{,}000 Criteo subsample its empirical coverage is 85.0%. We recommend prespecifying PPI++ with the exact variance as the primary analysis under random labeling and adequate labeled outcome counts, reading the diagnostic as a warning, not a certificate, and treating the surrogate index as a sensitivity analysis. Keywords: surrogate metrics, prediction-powered inference, causal inference, online experiments, A/B testing, variance reduction, treatment effect estimation, adaptive estimation 1 Introduction Online controlled experiments (A/B tests) are the primary tool for causal inference at technology companies, and each launch decision rests on an estimated effect on a “north-star” outcome such as long-term retention, cumulative revenue, or lifetime value. These outcomes may need 30, 60, or 90 days to mature, while decisions are due sooner. Units usually enroll on a rolling basis, so at any candidate decision date the outcome has matured for the earliest enrollees and is still censored for everyone else. Choosing when to decide is therefore choosing what fraction of outcomes to observe: waiting is costly, and deciding early means acting on the matured fraction plus short-term signals observed for every unit. This paper asks when that second option yields valid inference and how much precision it gains. Consider a retailer running an email-marketing experiment. Customers are randomized into campaign and control on a rolling basis over a four-week enrollment window, and the primary outcome is conversion, a purchase within two weeks of exposure. Funnel signals (a website visit, an add-to-cart event, a first-day click) arrive within a day or two. At a review in week 2.8, conversion windows have closed for roughly the first week of enrollees, two sevenths of the customers enrolled by that date, while every enrolled customer has funnel signals. The team can wait until week six, when every conversion window has closed, or call the experiment now from the matured conversions and everyone’s funnel signals (Figure 1 ); the Hillstrom analysis of Section 5 instantiates this structure on real data. A streaming service testing a recommendation algorithm against 90-day retention, with users onboarded over twelve weeks, faces the same choice at a month-four review: retention has matured for about a third of the sample, while first-week engagement is available for everyone. The analysis at a review conditions on the units enrolled by the review date, and the review date fixes the matured share π L \pi_{L} among them (Equation ( 1 )); we feature π L = 0.20 \pi_{L}=0.20 , a review at week 2.5 in the e-commerce example. Every coverage statement refers to a single pre-committed review date: calling the experiment at the first significant look of a continuously monitored test adds optional-stopping distortions, which anytime-valid variants of prediction-powered inference address ( Kilian et al., 2025 ) . The labeled fraction can also be a budget choice, when the outcome is expensive rather than slow (a survey, human labeling, or purchases matched from offline records), and it can then be large. We vary π L \pi_{L} from 0.05 to 1.00: small values are the calendar regime, and moderate-to-large values are where a plug-in variance paired with a coefficient below its optimum undercovers and the overlap correction matters most. In both readings the outcome must be defined for every randomized unit (a conversion indicator, or revenue per user including zeros); metrics defined only for converters raise a selection problem rather than a missing-label problem (Section 2.1 ). Two regimes look similar but rest on different assumptions. In the same-experiment delayed-label regime (Regime A), all units belong to one randomized experiment and the outcome has matured for a subset, as in both examples. In the historical-cohort regime (Regime B), the decision is due before any outcome from the current experiment has matured, so the prediction model must be trained on a prior cohort and transported, which requires comparable ( X , S ) (X,S) distributions, a stable conditional outcome model 𝔼 [ Y ∣ S , X ] \mathbb{E}[Y\mid S,X] , and similar treatment policies and treatment effects on the surrogate. Our formal results are stated for Regime A. DGP 4 (Section 3.1 ) probes one Regime B failure, a historical index that no longer transports. Regime B introduces additional transport assumptions, so the Regime A guarantees do not automatically extend to it, and the prediction model should be retrained on current labels whenever possible. calendar week 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 decision review (week 2.8) labeled ℒ \mathcal{L} : outcome matured unlabeled 𝒰 \mathcal{U} : surrogate only not yet enrolled: outside the sample surrogate window outcome window Figure 1: The timing problem in the e-commerce example. Each row is a cohort of customers, ordered by rolling enrollment over four weeks (dots mark exposure). Funnel surrogates (dark) arrive within days; the conversion window (light) takes two weeks. At the week-2.8 review seven of the ten cohorts have enrolled, every enrolled cohort’s surrogate window has closed, and the earliest two have matured; those two, two sevenths of the enrolled cohorts, form the labeled set ℒ \mathcal{L} . Enrolled but unmatured cohorts contribute surrogates only, and the three later cohorts (gray) have not enrolled and are outside the review-time sample. Regime A fits the prediction model on ℒ \mathcal{L} ; Regime B arises when the review precedes every outcome window, so the model must come from a prior cohort. This timing problem has motivated a substantial and increasingly interconnected literature on surrogate metrics : short-term proxy outcomes that correlate with the long-term target. Three traditions bear on this question, though recent work has shown they are converging. The statistical surrogacy literature includes the clinical-trial framework of Prentice (1989) ; subsequent econometric work develops surrogate-index methods for estimating long-term treatment effects. Athey et al. (2026) introduced the surrogate index for imputing long-term outcomes from short-term proxies, and Chen and Ritzwoller (2023) develop the corresponding semiparametric efficiency theory. Under the conditional-mean invariance 𝔼 [ Y | T , S , X ] = 𝔼 [ Y | S , X ] \mathbb{E}[Y|T,S,X]=\mathbb{E}[Y|S,X] of Assumption 2 , the index uses the full sample rather than the labeled subset and gains efficiency accordingly. When treatment and long-term outcomes are not jointly observed, the conditional-mean restriction cannot be checked directly in the available data. Transporting the outcome model to a new experiment requires additional assumptions. The invariance fails whenever treatment affects the outcome through channels that bypass the surrogate, which in practice is common. Prediction-powered inference (PPI, Angelopoulos et al., 2023a ; PPI++, Angelopoulos et al., 2023b ; recalibrated PPI, Ji et al., 2025 ) takes a different approach: rather than trusting the prediction model, it uses labeled data to correct for whatever systematic error the model introduces. The model-agnostic guarantee is both the strength and limitation of PPI: at the population-optimal tuning parameter its asymptotic variance is no larger than that of the labeled-only baseline, but the gain can be negligible in finite samples, and efficiency is bounded by prediction quality and conservative tuning. Mozer (2026) shows that PPI++ is structurally equivalent to the classical difference estimator ( Cassel et al., 1976 ) , connecting prediction-powered inference to decades of survey sampling theory. Ji et al. (2025) formally unify the surrogate index and PPI as endpoints of a bias–variance spectrum, establishing the theoretical foundation that our simulations characterize empirically. A third strand from the tech-industry experimentation literature has produced practical tools for surrogate selection and combination. Tripuraneni et al. (2024) construct composite proxies from historical experiments, calibrating weights across multiple surrogate metrics. Zito et al. (2025) develop Pareto-optimal proxy metrics. Duan et al. (2021) provide practical guidelines for surrogate metric use at scale. Industry methods construct proxies using historical experiments and explicit optimization objectives. Their targets and assumptions differ from the same-experiment treatment-effect estimand studied here. These literatures are converging theoretically, but each developed its tools in relative isolation: the surrogacy literature offers efficiency under strong assumptions, PPI robustness with limited efficiency, and the industry literature proxy-construction tools aimed at different targets. A systematic finite-sample comparison of the estimators under the failure modes that arise in practice (partial mediation, heterogeneous surrogate quality, temporal drift, outcome sparsity, nonlinear relationships, and antagonistic surrogates) has not, to our knowledge, been undertaken. Pre-experiment variance reduction such as CUPED ( Deng et al., 2013 ) and its machine-learning extensions ( Poyarkov et al., 2016 ) uses pre-treatment covariates and is complementary to the post-treatment surrogate methods studied here; surrogate methods add value beyond a CUPED-adjusted baseline (Section 4.1 ). The contributions, in decreasing order of what we believe is new, are a benchmark, a quantification of when violations are statistically invisible, and practitioner tools that apply established machinery to this setting: 1. A systematic finite-sample benchmark. Across seven estimators, eleven data-generating processes (DGPs), and 514 method-by-scenario cells in 93 simulation scenarios (primary configurations of Methods 0 to 5; the ablations of Appendix F.3 are not counted), with up to R = 2,000 R=2{,}000 replications per cell, the robustness–efficiency tradeoff is sharp. On the valid-surrogate DGPs 1 and 5, surrogate-based methods deliver large efficiency gains at small labeled fractions but lose coverage under moderate violations, while PPI-family methods stay valid under MCAR labeling at modest gains that shrink as the labeled fraction grows (Section 4.1 ). The tradeoff persists across the prediction model (OLS and gradient-boosted trees, GBT), the number of surrogates, and mild nonlinearity. The PPI side needs random labeling and adequate labeled outcome counts in each arm: it fails when the treatment effect drifts over the enrollment window (DGP 11, Section 4.4 ) and when labeled conversions are rare (Section 5.2 ). 2. The detection-damage gap, located. Specification pretests have low power against exactly the local violations that break inference ( Leeb and Pötscher, 2005 ; Guggenberger, 2010 ) ; practice needs the location of that blind spot. At π L = 0.20 \pi_{L}=0.20 we calibrate the band of violations that destroys surrogate-index coverage yet escapes an estimator-disagreement diagnostic on most datasets: ρ ∈ [ 0.09 , 0.37 ] \rho\in[0.09,0.37] at n = 10,000 n=10{,}000 and [ 0.03 , 0.16 ] [0.03,0.16] at n = 100,000 n=100{,}000 (Figure 5 ). Measured in the direct effect δ \delta , both edges shrink between the two sample sizes by ratios consistent with root- n n scaling, the damage edge less precisely located, so scale relocates the band rather than closing it; we claim the band for DGP 2, where we locate both edges, not universally (Section 4.3 ). Two industrial funnels show its two sides by analogy, not as points on the DGP 2 boundary. On Hillstrom (64,000 customers) the surrogate index carries 24.9% bias and covers 7.2% while the diagnostic rejects on 11% of splits; on Criteo (13.98 million users) the same within-funnel violation is detected, and subsampling traces detection turning on across two orders of magnitude of n n while the damage persists. A Criteo-calibrated semi-synthetic testbed, a multi-surrogate extension, and the LaLonde negative control complete the evidence (Section 5 ). 3. Practitioner tooling from established machinery. (a) The exact finite-sample variance of PPI++ in the all-units parameterization τ ^ Y ℒ + λ ⁡ ( τ ^ Y ^ all − τ ^ Y ^ ℒ ) \hat{\tau}_{Y}^{\mathcal{L}}+\lambda(\hat{\tau}_{\hat{Y}}^{\mathrm{all}}-\hat{\tau}_{\hat{Y}}^{\mathcal{L}}) at a fixed predictor and coefficient: the difference-estimator variance in that notation, which keeps the overlap covariance an independent-samples plug-in drops. This is bookkeeping for a reparameterization, not a defect in Angelopoulos et al. (2023b) , whose labeled-unlabeled form assigns the same variance (Section 2.4 ). (b) A joint asymptotic distribution for the surrogate index and PPI++ when the index is the learned linear one and every unit is scored out of fold (Proposition 3 ). It establishes first-order validity of the implemented OLS procedure, carries the first-stage uncertainty a fixed-predictor calculation omits, and supplies the standard error of the SI–PPI++ estimator-disagreement diagnostic, a Hausman (1978) -type test strictly weaker than a test of surrogacy (Sections 2.3 and 2.5 ). (c) A Cauchy-kernel hybrid, w = c / ( c + T n 2 ) w=c/(c+T_{n}^{2}) , in the frequentist model-averaging family of Hjort and Claeskens (2003) , whose local-asymptotic risk (Proposition 7 ) disciplines the tuning constant (Table A1 ). No adaptive weighting we study escapes the gap, and on Hillstrom the hybrid inherits 10.7% relative bias, so it is exploratory rather than a replacement for PPI++ (Appendix A ). 4. A prespecified primary analysis. Under MCAR labeling with adequate labeled outcome counts in each arm, the evidence supports PPI++ with the exact variance as the default primary analysis when surrogacy is uncertain, with the diagnostic as a warning rather than a certification of the surrogate-index interval (Section 6 ). Organization. Section 2 sets out the estimators and the formal results, Section 3 the eleven DGPs (Table 2 ) and the implementation of each design family (Table 3 ), Section 4 the simulation evidence, and Section 5 the public-data illustrations. Section 6 gives the workflow the results support and Section 7 the limitations. The appendices hold the hybrid estimator, the proofs, the diagnostic’s power grid, the Cross-PPI comparison, and the sensitivity analyses, ablations, and per-DGP results behind the main-text claims. 2 Setup and Methods 2.1 Notation, Estimands, and Sampling Regime Sampling regime (Regime A). All n n units belong to a single randomized experiment with T i ∼ iid Bernoulli ​ ( p ) T_{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{iid}}}{{\sim}}\text{Bernoulli}(p) for a known p ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) p\in(0,1) ; the surrogate S i S_{i} is observed for all units, and the primary outcome Y i Y_{i} for a subset chosen by a missing-completely-at-random (MCAR) labeling mechanism (Assumption 1 ). In this regime PPI++’s correction term has expectation zero at a fixed predictor, and the surrogate index, PPI++, and the hybrid share a common probability space. Missing-at-random (MAR) labeling does not by itself deliver that centering for the unweighted correction; the MAR variant of DGP 5 stresses it. The simulations set p = 0.5 p=0.5 ; the public-data analyses do not, and no formal result requires it. Units, treatment, and outcomes. For each unit i = 1 , … , n i=1,\ldots,n we observe a pre-treatment covariate vector X i ∈ ℝ p X_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} , a surrogate S i ∈ ℝ S_{i}\in\mathbb{R} (for all units), and a primary outcome Y i ∈ ℝ Y_{i}\in\mathbb{R} (for a labeled subset): in the e-commerce example a website visit and conversion, in the streaming example first-week engagement and 90-day retention. The main analysis takes S i S_{i} scalar; DGP 7 and the multi-surrogate testbed of Section 5.3 study several surrogates. The n n units are partitioned into a labeled set ℒ \mathcal{L} with | ℒ | = n L |\mathcal{L}|=n_{L} units where both ( S i , Y i ) (S_{i},Y_{i}) are observed, and an unlabeled set 𝒰 \mathcal{U} with | 𝒰 | = n U = n − n L |\mathcal{U}|=n_{U}=n-n_{L} units where only S i S_{i} is observed. We write n L , t = | { i ∈ ℒ : T i = t } | n_{L,t}=|\{i\in\mathcal{L}:T_{i}=t\}| for the number of labeled units in treatment arm t ∈ { 0 , 1 } t\in\{0,1\} . The labeled fraction π L = n L / n \pi_{L}=n_{L}/n is a key design parameter, where n n is the number of units enrolled by the review date. Under the calendar interpretation of Section 1 , π L \pi_{L} is pinned down by the review date: in the e-commerce example, with uniform enrollment over weeks 0 to 4 and a two-week outcome window, a review at week t t yields the matured share among units enrolled by the review, π L ​ ( t ) = t − 2 t ​ ( 2 ≤ t ≤ 4 ) , π L ​ ( t ) = t − 2 4 ​ ( 4 ≤ t ≤ 6 ) , \pi_{L}(t)=\frac{t-2}{t}\;\;(2\leq t\leq 4),\qquad\pi_{L}(t)=\frac{t-2}{4}\;\;(4\leq t\leq 6), (1) the second branch applying once enrollment has ended at week 4, so π L = 0.20 \pi_{L}=0.20 corresponds to a review at week 2.5 and π L = 1 \pi_{L}=1 to week 6. Under the label-budget interpretation, π L \pi_{L} is a cost choice. Under the Neyman–Rubin potential outcomes framework, each unit has potential outcomes ( S i ​ ( 0 ) , S i ​ ( 1 ) , Y i ​ ( 0 ) , Y i ​ ( 1 ) ) (S_{i}(0),S_{i}(1),Y_{i}(0),Y_{i}(1)) , and we assume SUTVA (stable unit treatment value assumption: no interference between units and no hidden versions of treatment). The primary estimand is the average treatment effect on the primary outcome: τ = 𝔼 ⁡ [ Y i ​ ( 1 ) − Y i ​ ( 0 ) ] . \tau=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0)]. (2) We also define the surrogate ATE τ S = 𝔼 ⁡ [ S i ​ ( 1 ) − S i ​ ( 0 ) ] \tau_{S}=\mathbb{E}[S_{i}(1)-S_{i}(0)] . A prediction model f ^ : ℝ 1 + p → ℝ \hat{f}:\mathbb{R}^{1+p}\to\mathbb{R} , estimated from the labeled set or auxiliary data, maps surrogate values and covariates to predicted primary outcomes: Y ^ i = f ^ ​ ( S i , X i ) \hat{Y}_{i}=\hat{f}(S_{i},X_{i}) . We make two formal assumptions. The first governs the labeling mechanism; the second defines the surrogacy condition that some methods require. Assumption 1 (MCAR labeling) . Membership in ℒ \mathcal{L} is independent of ( T i , S i , X i , Y i ) (T_{i},S_{i},X_{i},Y_{i}) , so outcomes are missing completely at random. The labeled set is drawn either by independent Bernoulli ⁡ ( π L ) \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi_{L}) indicators or as a uniformly random subset of fixed size ⌊ π L ​ n ⌋ \lfloor\pi_{L}n\rfloor , which is how our simulations draw it; every result below holds under either scheme. The covariates enter the statement because the prediction model uses them. We relax this in DGP 5 (Section 3.1 ). Under the calendar interpretation, where the labeled units are the earliest enrollees, Assumption 1 needs scrutiny. Randomization makes enrollment time independent of T i T_{i} , but MCAR also requires enrollment time to be unrelated to ( X i , S i , Y i ) (X_{i},S_{i},Y_{i}) : a stable user mix and a stable outcome process across the enrollment window. Seasonality, novelty effects, and drift in the enrolling population break this. DGP 11 labels the earliest-enrolled cohort under dialed drift (Section 4.4 ), DGP 5’s MAR variant stresses labeling through the surrogate, and DGP 4 stresses a surrogate–outcome relationship learned on a historical cohort. The public-data analyses of Section 5 mask labels at random, so MCAR holds there by construction. A second scope boundary separates three kinds of missingness. A well-defined outcome may be unobserved because its window has not closed or its measurement was not funded; that is the setting of Assumption 1 . A well-defined outcome may be observed with probability depending on post-treatment observables, as in DGP 5’s MAR variant, where labeled-only and PPI++ lose their design-based guarantee while AIPW with a correct observation model survives: across q q , relative bias runs from − 4.7 % -4.7\% to − 8.5 % -8.5\% for labeled-only, − 0.1 % -0.1\% to − 2.1 % -2.1\% for PPI++, and − 1.6 % -1.6\% to + 0.7 % +0.7\% for AIPW. Finally, some outcomes exist only for a treatment-dependent subpopulation: average order value or post-purchase satisfaction exist only for customers who convert, and conversion is what the campaign moves.
